items.title: Consumer Security Breach Notification Act
items.citation: D.C. Code § 28-3851 et seq. (Title 28, Chapter 38, Subchapter II)
items.applies_to_vendor: A person or entity that maintains, handles, or otherwise possesses personal information that it does not own or license (a vendor/service provider) must notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of the security of the system in the most expedient time possible following discovery, and must cooperate with the owner/licensee, including informing them of the date/nature of the breach and any remedial steps taken. The data owner then bears responsibility for notifying affected DC residents.
key_obligations: Third party/vendor holding data it does not own must notify the data owner or licensee of a breach 'in the most expedient time possible' following discovery, and must cooperate with the owner/licensee on remediation (D.C. Code § 28-3852(b))
Data owner/licensee must notify affected DC residents in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay
If a breach affects 50 or more DC residents, the entity must notify the DC Attorney General in the most expedient manner possible, and no later than when resident notice is given
A waiver of the subchapter's protections is void and unenforceable
items.notice_deadline: "the most expedient time possible following discovery" (vendor-to-owner notice); "most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" (owner-to-resident notice) — statute does not convert this to a fixed number of days
items.regulator_notice: DC Attorney General must be notified if a breach affects 50 or more District residents, in the most expedient manner possible and no later than when resident notice is provided (D.C. Code § 28-3852)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Definition is in D.C. Code § 28-3851(3), cross-referenced by § 28-3852; not independently re-fetched this session beyond what secondary summaries describe (SSN, driver's license/ID numbers, financial account numbers, and by 2020 amendment also biometric data, health/health-insurance information, taxpayer ID, and username/email plus password) — recommend a direct fetch of § 28-3851 to confirm exact wording.
items.penalties: The DC Attorney General may seek injunctive relief and restitution and recover a civil penalty not to exceed $100 per violation, plus costs and attorneys' fees (D.C. Code § 28-3853); a violation is also an unfair or deceptive trade practice under § 28-3904(kk); a DC resident injured by a violation has a private right of action for actual damages (excluding dignitary/pain-and-suffering damages), costs and attorneys' fees.
items.uncertainty: Fetched § 28-3852 directly from code.dccouncil.gov (official) this session and it supports the vendor-notification and AG-threshold language quoted above. The exact wording of the personal-information definition (§ 28-3851(3)) and the penalty section (§ 28-3853) were confirmed via search summaries referencing code.dccouncil.gov rather than a direct fetch of those two specific pages this session; the latest amendment year was not confirmed.

items.title: Protecting Students Digital Privacy Act of 2016
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds 'operators' of internet websites, online services, online applications, or mobile applications used primarily for K-12 school purposes and designed/marketed for that purpose. Operators must implement reasonable security, acknowledge LEA control of student data, delete personally identifiable student information within a reasonable time after termination of services, and notify the LEA of unauthorized access. Operators are barred from selling/renting/trading student data, targeted advertising using student data, or building non-educational profiles of students.
key_obligations: Operators must 'implement and maintain reasonable security policies and procedures appropriate to the nature of the personally identifiable student information'
Student information 'is under the control of the LEA' — operators may not treat it as their own
Operators must 'delete personally identifiable student information...within a reasonable period of time after termination or completion of services'
Operators must notify the LEA of 'unauthorized access to personally identifiable student information'
Operators may not 'sell, rent, or trade any personally identifiable student information' except in a business acquisition or with verified parental consent for specific educational purposes
Operators may not engage in targeted advertising based on information acquired through a student's use of the service
Operators may not use student data to build a non-educational profile of a student or group of students
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Chapter defines 'de-identified student information' as data from which all personally identifiable student information has been removed; also defines '1-to-1 device', '1-to-1 device provider', and '1-to-1 program' as devices provided to students for overnight/at-home use.
items.uncertainty: Fetched § 38-831.01 (definitions) and § 38-831.02 (operator obligations) directly from code.dccouncil.gov this session. Enforcement/penalty provisions for this chapter were not located/fetched this session, so penalties is left null rather than guessed.

DC has no comprehensive (CCPA/VCDPA-style) consumer privacy statute as of this session. Checked: DC OAG's own legislative announcement page (the Consumer Health Information Privacy Protection Act, CHIPPA, Bill B25-0930, was introduced by AG Schwalb in 2024 but died in committee in the 25th Council and covers only health data outside HIPAA, not a general comprehensive law); a search for any 2025/2026 DC Council bill establishing general consumer data rights (access/delete/opt-out) found none enacted. No official DC Council page confirming a passed comprehensive law was found.

items.title: Florida Information Protection Act of 2014 (FIPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: A 'third-party agent' — an entity contracted to maintain, store, or process personal information on behalf of a covered entity or governmental entity — must notify the covered entity of a breach as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 10 days following determination of the breach (or reason to believe the breach occurred). The covered entity then bears the duty to notify affected individuals and, above a threshold, the Florida Department of Legal Affairs (Attorney General).
key_obligations: Third-party agent must notify the covered entity 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 10 days following the determination of the breach'

Covered entity must notify the Florida Department of Legal Affairs when a breach affects 500 or more individuals in Florida, 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 30 days after the determination of the breach'
A violation is treated as an unfair or deceptive trade practice enforceable by the department under § 501.207
Civil penalties for late/failed notice: $1,000/day for the first 30 days, then $50,000 per 30-day period thereafter, up to $500,000 total, per breach (not per individual)
items.notice_deadline: third-party agent to covered entity: 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 10 days following the determination of the breach'; covered entity to Dept. of Legal Affairs: 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 30 days after the determination of the breach'
items.regulator_notice: Florida Department of Legal Affairs (Attorney General) must be notified when a breach affects 500 or more Florida individuals
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Includes SSN; government-issued ID numbers; financial account/card numbers with security codes; medical history/treatment information; health insurance policy numbers; biometric data; geolocation information — each combined with name, or username/email plus password.
items.penalties: Civil penalty of $1,000 per day for the first 30 days, then $50,000 per 30-day period (or portion) thereafter, capped at $500,000 for violations continuing beyond 180 days; penalty applies per breach, not per individual
items.effective_or_amended: 2023 (last amended by s. 25, ch. 2023-201; originally enacted 2014)
items.uncertainty: Fetched directly from flsenate.gov (official) this session; supports all fields above.

items.title: Florida Student Online Personal Information Protection Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds 'operators' of websites, online services, or applications used primarily for, and designed/marketed for, K-12 school purposes. Operators may not use covered student information for targeted advertising, may not share/sell/rent student information (with narrow exceptions), and may not use covered information to build a non-educational student profile. Operators must collect no more data than reasonably necessary, implement reasonable security, and delete covered information at the end of the course and no later than 90 days after a student's disenrollment (absent parental consent to retain).
key_obligations: Operators may not 'engage in targeted advertising...based on' covered information, even on third-party sites
Operators may not 'share, sell, or rent a student's information, including covered information' except for merger/acquisition compliance or with parental consent for national assessment providers
Operators may not 'use covered information...to amass a profile of a student, except in furtherance of K-12 school purposes'
Operators must 'collect no more covered information than is reasonably necessary'
Operators must 'implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices'
Operators must delete covered information 'at the conclusion of the course...and no later than 90 days' after student disenrollment, unless parent consents to retention
Violations are deceptive and unfair trade practices under Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, enforced exclusively by the Department of Legal Affairs
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Statute uses the term 'covered information' for student data collected by the operator; exact definitional boundaries not independently re-confirmed beyond the obligations fetched this session.
items.penalties: Enforced exclusively by the Florida Department of Legal Affairs as a deceptive/unfair trade practice; specific dollar penalty not located in the fetched text.
items.effective_or_amended: 2023 (amended; original enactment year not confirmed this session)
items.uncertainty: Fetched directly from flsenate.gov this session; breach-notification duties specific to this statute (if any) were not found in the fetched text, so left null rather than guessed.

items.title: Florida Digital Bill of Rights
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to 'controllers' that do business in Florida, collect personal data of Florida consumers (or have it collected on their behalf), determine the purposes/means of processing, and (a) have global gross annual revenue exceeding $1 billion, AND (b) meet at least one of: derive 50%+ of global gross annual revenue from online advertising sales, operate a smart-speaker/voice-assistant service, or operate an app store/digital distribution platform offering 250,000+ applications. A 'processor' (LOVELEEDAY, acting on a qualifying controller's behalf) must cooperate with the controller's compliance duties, follow the controller's instructions under a data-processing contract, keep data confidential, assist with security and breach-notification obligations, delete or return personal data on request at service completion (unless retention is legally required), bind subcontractors to the same terms, and allow the controller to assess compliance.
key_obligations: Processor 'must assist the controller in meeting or complying with the controller's duties,' including consumer-rights requests and breach notification
A written contract must set out 'clear instructions for processing data,' the nature/purpose, data types, duration, and both parties' rights/obligations
Processor must ensure 'each person processing personal data is subject to a duty of confidentiality'
Processor must 'delete or return all personal data to the controller as requested' at service completion, unless retention is legally required
Processor may only 'engage any subcontractor pursuant to a written contract' imposing the same requirements
Processor must allow 'reasonable assessments by the controller' and provide information needed to demonstrate compliance
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Applicability is unusually narrow and revenue/business-model-gated (>$1B global revenue plus an ad-tech/smart-speaker/app-store condition) — this is a materially higher bar than CCPA/VCDPA-style laws and will exclude most LOVELEEDAY clients and LOVELEEDAY itself from direct 'controller' status; LOVELEEDAY could still be a 'processor' under contract with a qualifying controller-client.
items.penalties: Enforcement section (§ 501.715 references penalty under a cross-referenced section) could not be fully located this session; general secondary reporting (not verified as source_url) describes exclusive Attorney General enforcement with a cure period, but the exact section number, cure period length, and civil penalty amount were not confirmed against the official text this session.
items.effective_or_amended: 2023 enactment (Fla. SB/HB 262); effective July 1, 2024 per widely reported secondary sources — not independently re-confirmed against the official statute text this session
items.uncertainty: Fetched § 501.712 (processor duties) and § 501.702 (applicability/controller definition) directly from flsenate.gov and both support the fields above. Could NOT locate/fetch the specific enforcement/penalty section (guessed section numbers 501.715, 501.717, 501.720 did not contain it) or independently confirm the effective date this session — marked verified:false because those two fields rely on unconfirmed secondary knowledge rather than a fetched official page.

items.title: Georgia Personal Identity Protection Act
items.applies_to_vendor: An 'information broker' or other person/entity that maintains computerized data that includes personal information on behalf of another data collector (the data owner) must, per secondary reporting, notify the data owner/licensee promptly upon discovering that a breach may have occurred; the data owner then bears the duty to notify affected Georgia residents.
key_obligations: Information brokers/custodians must notify the data owner/licensee of a suspected breach so the owner can notify residents (per secondary sources; exact statutory subsection and timing not independently confirmed against official text this session)
For breaches affecting 10,000 or more Georgia residents, notice must also go to nationwide consumer reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) without unreasonable delay
'Data collectors' (certain state/local government agencies) and 'information brokers' are the entities covered by the notice duty
items.notice_deadline: Secondary sources describe a 24-hour information-broker-to-data-owner window; this specific number could not be confirmed against the official O.C.G.A. text this session and should be treated as unverified.
items.uncertainty: Georgia's official code (O.C.G.A.) is published online only through a LexisNexis-hosted portal under contract with the Georgia Code Revision Commission (lexisnexis.com/hottopics/gacode/); this is a JavaScript single-page application that returned only a tracking pixel to automated fetch tools this session (both WebFetch and curl), so the statute text could not be directly confirmed against the official source. All facts above are drawn from secondary legal-reference sites (Justia, Sentra, LegalClarity) that reproduce the O.C.G.A. text (which is not copyrightable per Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org) but are not themselves the official publisher. Treat the 24-hour notice figure and penalty details as unconfirmed.

items.title: Student Data Privacy, Accessibility, and Transparency Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Defines an 'operator' as any entity (other than the Department of Education, local boards, the Georgia Student Finance Commission, or schools) that operates a website/online service/application with actual knowledge it is used for, and designed/marketed for, K-12 school purposes. The Act bans operators from targeted advertising using student data, creating non-school student profiles, and selling student data, and restricts collection of student political/economic/religious data and reporting of juvenile-delinquency/criminal/medical data.
key_obligations: Operators may not use student data for targeted advertising
Operators may not create student profiles for non-school reasons
Operators may not sell student data
Restrictions apply to collection of student political, economic, and religious information
Restrictions apply to reporting of juvenile delinquency, criminal records, and medical/health records
A senior Georgia DOE staff member is designated chief privacy officer responsible for agency data-protection policy
items.uncertainty: Same limitation as the Georgia breach item: the official LexisNexis-hosted O.C.G.A. portal is a JavaScript application not readable by automated fetch tools this session. Facts drawn from the Georgia Department of Education's own summary page (georgiainsights.gadoe.org, an official state agency source, though not the codified text itself) and Justia's reproduction of the statute. Penalty/enforcement provisions for this specific Article were not located this session.

items.title: Security Breach of Personal Information
items.applies_to_vendor: A business or government agency that owns or licenses personal information of Hawaii residents must give written notice to the Office of Consumer Protection when a breach affects 1,000 or more Hawaii residents (HRS § 487N-2(f), confirmed via the Office of Consumer Protection's own page). Secondary sources describe a further duty for any person/business that merely maintains (does not own) computerized personal information to notify the owner/licensee upon discovery of a breach, but the exact statutory subsection and wording could not be fetched from the official HRS text this session.
key_obligations: A business/agency owning or licensing Hawaii residents' personal information must give written notice to the Office of Consumer Protection when 1,000+ Hawaii residents are affected (HRS § 487N-2(f))
A non-owning custodian of data is understood (per secondary sources) to owe a notice duty to the data owner, but this was not confirmed against the official statute this session
items.regulator_notice: Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (Dept. of Commerce and Consumer Affairs) must receive written notice when a breach affects 1,000 or more Hawaii residents (HRS § 487N-2(f))
items.uncertainty: The official Hawaii Revised Statutes site (capitol.hawaii.gov) returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare block) to both WebFetch and curl this session and could not be read. The regulator-notice threshold (1,000 residents, HRS § 487N-2(f)) was confirmed directly from the Hawaii DCCA Office of Consumer Protection's own official page (cca.hawaii.gov), which is an official state-agency source. The vendor-to-owner notification duty, exact timing wording, and personal-information definition were not confirmed against the official text this session and should not be treated as verified.

items.title: Student data privacy / educational technology operator restrictions
items.applies_to_vendor: Per the Future of Privacy Forum's state-law tracker, Hawaii's law is SOPIPA-style and limits how an operator of a website/online service/application working with the Department of Education may use student data: operators must have security procedures in place and delete information within a reasonable time, and may disclose information for legitimate research purposes.
key_obligations: Operators working with the Dept. of Education must limit use of student data consistent with a SOPIPA-style framework
Operators must have security procedures in place
Operators must delete student information within a reasonable time
Operators may disclose information for legitimate research purposes
items.uncertainty: The official Hawaii Revised Statutes site returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare block) to automated fetch tools this session and could not be read directly, so the exact statutory text/section could not be confirmed against the official source. Citation and obligations are drawn from the Future of Privacy Forum's state student-privacy-law tracker, a reputable non-official secondary source.

items.title: Idaho data breach notification law
items.applies_to_vendor: An agency, individual, or commercial entity that maintains computerized data including personal information it does NOT own or license must 'give notice to and cooperate with the owner or licensee of the information of any breach' immediately following discovery, if misuse of the information about an Idaho resident has occurred or is reasonably likely to occur (Idaho Code § 28-51-105(2)).
key_obligations: A non-owning maintainer of data must 'give notice to and cooperate with the owner or licensee' of any breach 'immediately following discovery' where misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely
State agencies must notify the Idaho Attorney General's office within 24 hours of discovering a breach; a commercial entity may notify the AG but is not required to
General notification to affected residents must occur 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay,' balanced against law-enforcement needs and restoring system integrity
Notice is not required if a reasonable investigation determines misuse has not occurred and is not reasonably likely to occur
Enforcement: the state's regulators may bring a civil action for injunctive relief; intentional failure to provide required notice carries a fine of up to $25,000 per breach
items.notice_deadline: 'immediately following discovery' (vendor-to-owner notice); 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay' (owner-to-resident notice); 'within twenty-four (24) hours' (state agency to Idaho AG)
items.regulator_notice: State agencies must notify the Idaho Attorney General within 24 hours of discovery; commercial entities may notify but are not required to
items.personal_info_definition_notes: An Idaho resident's first name/initial and last name combined with SSN, driver's license/Idaho ID card number, or account/credit/debit card number plus any required security code/access code/password; publicly available government-record or media information is excluded.
items.penalties: Fine of not more than $25,000 per breach for intentional failure to provide required notice; regulators may bring a civil action to enforce compliance and enjoin further violations (Idaho Code § 28-51-107)
items.uncertainty: Fetched §§ 28-51-104, 28-51-105, and 28-51-107 directly from legislature.idaho.gov (official) this session; all fields above are supported by that text. Latest amendment year not shown in the fetched excerpts.

items.title: Student data — definitions, use and limitations, penalties
items.citation: Idaho Code § 33-133 (enacted via SB 1372, Student Data Accessibility, Transparency and Accountability Act, 2014)
items.applies_to_vendor: Vendor contracts governing databases, online services, assessments, or instructional supports that include student data and are outsourced to private vendors must include express provisions safeguarding privacy/security and restricting secondary uses. A vendor contract must either (1) prohibit any secondary use of student data (sales, marketing, advertising — allowing only processing for service maintenance), or (2) disclose in detail any secondary uses and obtain express parental consent for them. Vendors may use aggregated (de-identified) data without restriction. Contracts must include data-destruction-date provisions and penalties for noncompliance.
key_obligations: Access to the student data system is restricted to vendors who require it to perform assigned duties
Vendor contracts must prohibit secondary uses (sales/marketing/advertising) OR require detailed disclosure plus express parental consent for any secondary use
Vendor contracts must include data-destruction-date provisions and specific use restrictions
Vendor contracts must include penalties for noncompliance
The State Board of Education must perform routine compliance audits (FERPA and other privacy laws)
Enforceable by the Idaho Attorney General
items.penalties: Civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation for individuals/vendors violating the statute or related rules, or for school districts failing to adopt required policies where improper data release occurs; penalties are recovered through civil enforcement and deposited into the state general fund.
items.uncertainty: Fetched directly from legislature.idaho.gov (official) this session; supports the fields above.

No official Idaho Legislature source was fetched confirming the absence of a bill in the current session, so this is based on secondary reporting only.

items.title: Personal Information Protection Act
items.applies_to_vendor: A 'data collector' that maintains or stores, but does not own or license, computerized data including personal information must notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach 'immediately following discovery,' if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person, and must cooperate with the owner/licensee, including informing them of the breach date/nature and steps taken or planned (815 ILCS 530/12(b)).
key_obligations: Non-owning data collector must notify the owner/licensee of a breach 'immediately following discovery' and cooperate with the owner/licensee on remediation (815 ILCS 530/12(b))
Owning/licensing data collector must notify affected Illinois residents 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay' (815 ILCS 530/10(a))
Notification to residents may be delayed at the written request of law enforcement if it would interfere with a criminal investigation, but must occur once that interference ends

Data collectors required to notify more than 500 Illinois residents from a single breach must also notify the Illinois Attorney General, including a description of the breach, number of residents affected, and remedial steps (815 ILCS 530/10(e))
A violation of the Act constitutes an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act (815 ILCS 530/20)
Any waiver of the Act's provisions is void and unenforceable as against public policy (815 ILCS 530/15)
State agencies must submit a breach report to the General Assembly within 5 business days of discovery/notification (815 ILCS 530/25)
items.notice_deadline: vendor-to-owner: 'immediately following discovery'; owner-to-resident: 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay'
items.regulator_notice: Illinois Attorney General must be notified when notice is required to more than 500 Illinois residents from a single breach (815 ILCS 530/10(e)); exempt for HIPAA-covered entities/business associates in compliance with 815 ILCS 530/50
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Name combined with SSN; driver's license/State ID number; financial account or credit/debit card number (with any required security code/access code/password); medical information; health insurance information; or unique biometric data generated from measurements/technical analysis of body characteristics — each qualifying where the name or data element is unencrypted/unredacted, or the decryption key was also compromised.
items.penalties: A violation is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act (enforced by the Illinois Attorney General); no separate fixed civil-penalty figure appears in this Act itself.
items.effective_or_amended: 2017 (amendments per P.A. 99-503, eff. 1-1-17, cited in the fetched text; later amendments exist but not all confirmed this session)
items.uncertainty: Fetched the full Act text directly from ilga.gov (official) this session via curl (WebFetch could not validate ilga.gov's TLS certificate; curl with certificate verification disabled was used to retrieve the same public page, which quoted section numbers/citations verbatim in-page).

items.title: Student Online Personal Protection Act (SOPPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds 'operators' providing school services to K-12 schools under a written agreement. Operators may not knowingly engage in targeted advertising using information (including covered information and persistent identifiers) acquired through K-12 use of the site/service; may not amass a non-school student profile; and may not sell or rent student information (with a carve-out for merger/acquisition where the successor complies with the Act). Written agreements must state how covered information will be deleted or transferred to the school once no longer needed, and must specify the timeframe.
key_obligations: Operator may not 'engage in targeted advertising' based on covered information/persistent identifiers acquired through K-12 school use (105 ILCS 85/10(1))
Operator may not use such information 'to amass a profile about a student,' except in furtherance of K-12 school purposes (105 ILCS 85/10(2))
Operator may not 'sell or rent a student's information, including covered information' (105 ILCS 85/10(3)), subject to a merger/acquisition carve-out
Written agreements between school and operator must state that the operator must delete or transfer to the school all covered information once no longer needed, within a specified time period
Agreements must describe cost/expense allocation between school and operator if a breach is attributed to the operator, including notification and credit-monitoring costs
Violations are unlawful practices enforceable by the Illinois Attorney General under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act (105 ILCS 85/35)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Uses the term 'covered information'; also restricts retention of a student's online activity/requests for the purpose of targeting subsequent ads.
items.penalties: Violations are unlawful practices under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act; the Illinois Attorney General may take appropriate action (105 ILCS 85/35). No separate fixed civil-penalty figure appears in this Act.
items.uncertainty: Fetched the full Act text directly from ilga.gov (official) this session via curl (TLS verification disabled due to a certificate error on ilga.gov itself, not a proxy/mirror).

items.title: Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to any 'private entity' (including a vendor like LOVELEEDAY) that collects, captures, purchases, receives through trade, or otherwise obtains a person's biometric identifier or biometric information (e.g., fingerprints, retina/iris scans, voiceprints, hand/face geometry scans). Before doing so, the private entity must (1) inform the subject in writing that biometric data is being collected/stored, (2) inform the subject in writing of the specific purpose and length of term of collection/storage/use, and (3) receive a written release from the subject. The entity must publish a written retention schedule and destruction guidelines, may not sell/lease/trade/profit from the data, and may only disclose it with consent, to complete a subject-requested transaction, as required by law, or pursuant to a valid warrant/subpoena.
key_obligations: Written retention policy, made public, must set a retention schedule and destruction guidelines; biometric data must be permanently destroyed when the initial collection purpose is satisfied or within 3 years of the individual's last interaction, whichever comes first (740 ILCS 14/15(a))

Before collection, a private entity must (1) inform the subject in writing that data is being collected/stored, (2) inform the subject in writing of the specific purpose and length of term, and (3) obtain a written release (740 ILCS 14/15(b))
A private entity may not 'sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from' a person's biometric identifier/information (740 ILCS 14/15(c))

Disclosure/redisclosure is barred unless the subject consents, the disclosure completes a subject-requested/authorized financial transaction, disclosure is required by law, or is pursuant to a valid warrant/subpoena (740 ILCS 14/15(d))

Private entities must protect biometric data using the reasonable standard of care within their industry, and in a manner at least as protective as they use for other confidential/sensitive information

Any person aggrieved by a violation has a private right of action in state circuit court (or as a supplemental federal claim): $1,000 or actual damages (whichever is greater) for a negligent violation; $5,000 or actual damages (whichever is greater) for an intentional or reckless violation; plus reasonable attorneys' fees, costs (including expert witness fees), and other relief including injunctive relief (740 ILCS 14/20)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Covers 'biometric identifiers' (retina/iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, hand/face geometry scan) and 'biometric information' derived from them; excludes writing samples, signatures, photographs, physical descriptions, and certain health-care/testing records covered by other law.
items.penalties: Private right of action: $1,000 (negligent) or $5,000 (intentional/reckless) liquidated damages per violation, or actual damages if greater, plus attorneys' fees/costs and possible injunctive relief (740 ILCS 14/20). A 2024 amendment (P.A. 103-769, eff. 8-2-24) changed damages accrual to a single violation per person per collection method rather than per-scan, significantly narrowing per-incident exposure.
items.uncertainty: Fetched the full Act text directly from ilga.gov (official) this session via curl (TLS verification disabled due to a certificate error on ilga.gov itself). The 2024 damages-accrual amendment is noted based on the amendment citation ('Source: P.A. 103-769, eff. 8-2-24') appearing in the fetched official text, though the full substantive text of that amendment was not separately quoted.

items.title: Disclosure of Security Breach
items.applies_to_vendor: A person that maintains computerized data but is not a 'data base owner' must notify the data base owner if the person discovers that personal information was, or may have been, acquired by an unauthorized person. The data base owner then must disclose the breach to affected Indiana residents, and — if disclosure is required to more than 1,000 consumers — must also notify each nationwide consumer reporting agency and the Indiana Attorney General.
key_obligations: A non-owner maintainer of data must notify the data base owner upon discovering that personal information was or may have been acquired by an unauthorized person

The data base owner must disclose the breach to an Indiana resident whose unencrypted (or encrypted-with-compromised-key) personal information was or may have been acquired, where the owner knows or should know the acquisition has resulted in or could result in identity deception, identity theft, or fraud
If disclosure is required to more than 1,000 consumers, the data base owner must also notify each nationwide consumer reporting agency with information to help prevent fraud
If the data base owner makes a disclosure, it must also disclose the breach to the Indiana Attorney General
items.regulator_notice: Indiana Attorney General must be notified whenever the data base owner makes a disclosure to Indiana residents (per secondary summary of Ind. Code art. 24-4.9; exact section number and timing not confirmed against official text this session)
items.uncertainty: Indiana's official code site (iga.in.gov) is a JavaScript single-page application that returns no server-rendered statutory text to automated fetch tools (confirmed via both WebFetch and curl this session — curl returned only the React app shell); the site's backing API (api.iga.in.gov) requires an API key not available this session. All facts above are drawn from a WebSearch summary referencing law.justia.com's reproduction of the Indiana Code, which is not the official publisher. Exact timing language, PI definition, and penalty amounts are unconfirmed.

Could not confirm a SOPIPA-style Indiana statute that binds operators/vendors of educational technology directly. Checked: the Future of Privacy Forum's comprehensive state student-privacy-law tracker (fpf.org/student-privacy-state-laws/) does not list Indiana among the states with such a law. A secondary source (CaseGuard) references 'Indiana HB 1003' (2014) but describes only educator/school duties (using student data solely for educational purposes, retention limits, data security plans, protecting the state longitudinal data system) rather than direct operator/vendor obligations, and no codified Indiana Code citation could be confirmed for it this session. Indiana University's own student-privacy page cites only federal FERPA, not a state student-privacy statute. Marking exists:false rather than guessing a citation; this should be revisited if a specific vendor-binding Indiana Code section is later identified.

items.title: Indiana Consumer Data Protection Act (ICDPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: Establishes 'controller' and 'processor' roles. A processor's data-processing activities must be governed by a binding contract with the controller that clearly sets out processing instructions, the nature and purpose of processing, the type of data processed, the duration of processing, and both parties' rights and obligations; the processor must adhere to the controller's instructions and assist the controller in meeting its obligations (consumer rights requests, security, and breach notification under Indiana's existing breach statute).
key_obligations: Processor must operate under a contract with the controller specifying instructions, purpose, data types, duration, and rights/obligations of both parties
Processor must follow the controller's instructions and assist with the controller's compliance duties, including consumer requests, security, and breach notification support

Enforcement is by the Indiana Attorney General exclusively; per secondary reporting, the AG must give written notice of alleged violations and a 30-day opportunity to cure before an enforcement action, with civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation if uncured (not independently confirmed against the official text this session)
items.regulator_notice: Indiana Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority (per secondary reporting; not independently confirmed against official text this session)
items.penalties: Per secondary reporting (not confirmed against the official text this session): injunctive relief and a civil penalty of up to $7,500 per violation, after a 30-day cure opportunity.
items.uncertainty: The official iga.in.gov PDF for Title 24, Article 15 could not be retrieved this session — the URL is served by Indiana's JavaScript single-page application rather than a static PDF (curl returned only the React app shell, ~690 bytes), and iga.in.gov's backing JSON API (api.iga.in.gov) requires an API key not available this session. All facts above are drawn from WebSearch summaries citing law.justia.com and privacy-law secondary sources, not the official code. Effective date (Jan. 1, 2026) is widely reported but not independently confirmed against the official text.
